title: On the TOBA singers were the stars, not the bands
summary: He explains that blues singers and comedians were the attraction, soloists had little room, and territory bands played elsewhere.

bands.name: Andy Kirk and His Clouds of Joy

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: You know, Danny, during those years singers were the principals. You don't think that Coleman Hawkins could take his tenor saxophone player and go out and stand in front of Butter-Beans and Susie and be the star. He was just another musician in the background. Maybe they'd let him play a number. Maybe. Or he'd have an opportunity when they did have an

opportunity to play was when the chorus girls...you know, you could really do your thing and play as hard as you wanted to which would be an inspiration to the chorus girls. But other than that they didn't have, you know, very seldom would you have a band that was the attraction. I can't even remember when they ever did that on the TOBA. And it's quite possible, but I'm telling you from my knowledge what they would do. They would...a guy would come on the show...he could play when the chorus girls were dancing, you know what I mean, he could, you know, do his thing. But when George Williams and Bessie Brown come out to sing one of those songs that Ida Cox was singing...a solo, Bessie singing the "Backwater Blues," there was no place for a soloist, 'cause James P. had set the tone and set a precedent. And very rarely did people improvise from that original format. You know, you had bands Like McKinney's Cotton Pickers—speaking of McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Fletcher Henderson... they played dances. Not in the South. They didn't play too many dances in the South because there were not too many places for them to play to promote them. Local bands like the Blue Devils...Territory Bands, I guess they called them...Alphonso Trent, Troy Floyd, Bennie Long, Bennie Moten and then he was sort of like a big time band ...what's this other boy's name, Twelve

Clouds of Joy, Andy Kirk, you know, these guys were the Territory Bands that really, you know, played, but you very rarely saw Duke Ellington in Dallas, you know, during that period. He may play New York or Chicago or the Cotton Club or something and then go to California to Sebastian's or something like that. And then in 1927, when the Regal Theater opened, you know what I mean, they'd have a show. But they always had to have that original TOBA format of a comedian, Pigmeat Markham, you know what I mean, Pigmeat, Bert Williams, but Bud didn't play too many black theaters, but that kind of thing. And then they also had like Trixie Smith, Ida Cox, Mamie Smith, Eldora Williams, you know, and them blues singers. Now each one of these blues singers would have a person with them who played exclusively for them. Like Ida Cox would have Jesse Crump. Now Ma Rainey had Dorsey.* George Williams and Bessie Brown, they used like the show piano player and...what's that other guy's name...Butter Beans and Susie used the show piano player. But you very rarely had, like stars. Now Pinetop Smith (unintelligible) was on the shows, you know what I mean. He played all the shows. It's too bad he got killed so early because he was really something to behold. He was playing that very simple Boogie-Woogie. But you know, the thing that amazed me, in Chicago,
*Thomas A. Dorsey, then known as "Georgia Tom." Dorsey went on to compose the popular and well known Gospel hymn, "Precious Lord."
this guy that worked at the ball park...what's his name...

How in the hell he became so famous. And never... I never saw him anyplace. I don't think I ever saw Jim. I saw him maybe...I was out at the ball park with Mayo, but I never heard him play. Now how can things like that happen?
I don't know. He didn't make any records until...
